titolo: Why Did Spain Rule the Philippines for 300 Years but Leave Almost No Spanish?

numero.sotto: YEARS OF SPANISH RULE, ALMOST NO SPEAKERS

descrizione:
Spain ruled Mexico for 300 years and Mexico speaks Spanish. It ruled the Philippines for 333 years, and almost nobody there speaks it today. What happened? We follow the Manila galleons, a few thousand settlers, hundreds of languages, and friars who guarded their own power.

Then came the American teachers, the destruction of Manila in 1945, and the surprising Spanish words that Filipinos still use every day, from the clock to the calendar to their own surnames.
tag: why philippines does not speak spanish

scene.testo: Spain ruled the Philippines for 333 years. Almost nobody there speaks Spanish. A ship of American teachers. A city wiped out. And friars who blocked their own king. Why?
Spain ruled Mexico for 300 years, and Mexico speaks Spanish. Peru, Colombia, Cuba, Chile too. So why is the Philippines the exception?
Spain held these islands for 333 years, longer than it held Mexico. Yet land in Manila and speak Spanish, and you get blank looks.
Fewer than half a percent of Filipinos speak it well. You might guess the Americans swapped it for English in 1898.
That is only part of it. Spanish was barely spoken even while Spain was in charge, and some Spaniards themselves stopped it spreading.
To see why, look at the map. The Philippines is about as far from Madrid as you can possibly get.
In 1565, Miguel López de Legazpi set up camp on the island of Cebu. He had sailed from Mexico, and that detail matters a lot.
That same year, the friar and navigator Andrés de Urdaneta found a way to sail back east across the Pacific.

eventi.descrizione: 16th-century Spanish friar and navigator, tonsure, dark habit

scene.testo: That opened the Manila galleon route. For 250 years, one or two ships a year sailed between Manila and Acapulco.

eventi.testo: One or two ships a year

scene.testo: Each crossing took around four months. For most of that time, the islands were run from Mexico City, not from Spain.
So the islands were a colony of a colony, hanging at the far end of a very long rope.

eventi.testo: A very long chain of command

scene.testo: That distance decided who went there, and the answer is hardly anyone. In the 1600s, only about 600 settlers came from Spain itself.
One estimate counts about 15,600 settlers from Mexico and Peru. The islands themselves held roughly 667,000 people.
Most of those settlers stayed in or around Manila. A Filipino farmer could go a whole life without meeting a Spanish speaker.
In Mexico, Spanish speakers spread across towns, farms, and mines. Spanish became the language people used every day, everywhere.
Then there is the geography. The Philippines has more than 7,000 islands, and before the Spanish came, they did not share one language.
Over 100 languages are still spoken there today. Mountains and sea kept every island group, and sometimes every valley, apart.
For a tiny colonial government, that was a nightmare. The obvious fix was to teach everyone Spanish so they had something in common.
Spain's kings agreed. Over the centuries, the crown sent order after order saying the locals must learn Spanish. Most went nowhere.
To see why, meet the people who really ran the islands. Outside Manila, Spain barely had a government at all.
What it had were friars, Catholic missionaries from the Augustinians, Franciscans, Dominicans, and Jesuits. In many towns, the friar was the only Spaniard anyone saw.

eventi.testo: The friar was the only Spaniard

scene.testo: Spaniards were banned from living in native villages unless they were friars. So the friar was the government, the school, and the church at once.
To convert people, friars learned local languages, and the crown required it. In 1593, one of the first books printed there was in Spanish and Tagalog.
Over time, many friars noticed something. Being the only person who spoke both languages gave them real power.
A villager with a complaint about a tax or a landlord went through the friar. A Spanish official's message went through him, too.
If everyone learned Spanish, nobody would need the friar. Some also feared that readers would find Spanish ideas about rights and equality.
So when orders came to teach the language, many friars dragged their feet or quietly ignored them. That surprised me most.

eventi.testo: Friars slowed their own king's plan

scene.testo: One of the biggest brakes on Spanish in the Philippines was Spain's own missionaries.
In 1863, Spain finally opened free public primary schools taught in Spanish. Even then, fewer than 3 percent of Filipinos could speak it.
By the end of Spanish rule, estimates ranged from 3 to 10 percent. Almost all were educated people living in towns.
Yet that small group made it count. Filipinos like Jose Rizal wrote books and newspapers in Spanish. They were called the ilustrados.

eventi.descrizione: 19th-century Filipino doctor and writer, round glasses, dark suit

eventi.testo: The enlightened ones wrote in Spanish

scene.testo: They used Spanish to push for reform and then independence. On June 12, 1898, Emilio Aguinaldo declared independence in Spanish.
The new republic even wrote its government in Spanish. By 1898, it was becoming the language of a Filipino nation, at least among its leaders.
Then the Americans arrived. In May 1898, a US fleet destroyed the Spanish fleet in Manila Bay.
After the war, Spain handed the islands to the United States. The Americans then fought the new Filipino republic until 1902.

eventi.testo: Spain handed islands to the US

scene.testo: That war cost hundreds of thousands of lives. Once in control, America did what Spain never managed. It went after the schools.
In July 1901, a US Army transport called the Thomas left San Francisco carrying about 500 American teachers.
It stopped in Hawaii and reached Manila on August 21. Filipinos called the teachers the Thomasites, after the ship.
By 1902, over a thousand American teachers were in the islands. They took over the schools Spain had started and switched them to English.
Spain had relied on about 2,000 clergy, many unwilling to share their language. America sent teachers whose whole job was to spread theirs.
English was also the key to jobs in the new government, giving every family a reason to learn it.
It worked fast. Within a couple of generations, English was the language of school, law, and business.
Spanish did not vanish at once. It stayed official alongside English, and old families in parts of Manila kept speaking it at home.
Then came the Second World War. In February 1945, American and Japanese forces fought street by street for Manila.
Around 100,000 civilians were killed. By some counts, Manila became the second most destroyed city of the war, after Warsaw.
The worst fighting hit Intramuros, Ermita, and Malate. According to historian Florentino Rodao, only there was Spanish still the everyday street language.

eventi.descrizione: Spanish historian of the Philippines, glasses, grey hair

scene.testo: Hundreds of Spaniards died, along with many Filipino families who spoke Spanish at home. The neighborhoods that kept the language alive were gone.
After that, Spanish faded quickly. In 1987, a new constitution dropped it as an official language.
Today, around 400,000 Filipinos speak it well. In a country of over 100 million, that is a tiny fraction.

eventi.testo: A tiny fraction of the country

scene.testo: That sounds like the end of the story. Except Filipinos still use Spanish every day without noticing.

eventi.testo: Spanish lives on in daily speech

scene.testo: Ask the time in Manila and you will hear alas dos for 2:00, from the Spanish. Prices use Spanish numbers too, so 12 pesos is dos.
Six of the seven days of the week in Tagalog come from Spanish, and all twelve months do.
Tagalog holds thousands of Spanish words, like mesa for table, kotse for car, and pamilya for family.
Then there are surnames. In 1849, Governor Narciso Claveria ordered families to pick fixed surnames from an official catalog, mostly Spanish.
That is why so many Filipinos are named Santos, Reyes, or de la Cruz without a drop of Spanish ancestry.
And in Zamboanga, at the southwestern tip of Mindanao, people speak Chavacano, a language of Spanish words with local grammar.
It is the only Spanish-based Creole in Asia. Roughly a million people still speak it, though counts vary.
Compare that with Mexico, where about 99 in 100 people speak Spanish. Same empire, same centuries, utterly different result.
So Spain spent 333 years in the Philippines and never got most people speaking Spanish. Its words got in anyway, through the clock, the calendar, and people's own names.
A Filipino who says they speak no Spanish has probably used a dozen Spanish words before lunch. Next time, why Brazil was only meant to be a thin strip of coast.
